title: Chapter 58 – Pool Stage
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

Jian has made a great many plans in his life, and this is the first one in which he is the bait.

He sits on the edge of the reservoir, with his feet in the water, and waits.

The pool is full again. It has been full for six days, ever since the red haze thinned and the beds drank back what had been taken from them, and it glows a soft, deep, living green, like a lamp seen through a leaf. The mist rises off it in slow gray coils. It is very cold. He has been sitting with his ankles in it for an hour, and cannot feel his toes, and does not mind. The cold keeps him awake.

Pebble is in his lap. She has lost two more scales since the cellar, and her back, under his hand, is a patchwork of pale, bare, pearly places, like the bald spots in an old rug. She is not asleep. She lies with her small head on his knee, and her round black eyes open, and she watches the dark where the seam is.

Is he coming? she says.

Yes.

How do you know?

Because I would.

It is not a clever answer. It is simply the truest one he has. If he were an old man with sixty years of patience and a dying master, and the one door in the world that he had wanted had opened under his hand, and a child had left a seam open behind him like a candle in a window, he would come. He would come with every man he had. He would not stop to ask why it was so easy.

That is the thing about a good trap, he thinks. It must look exactly like a gift.

* * *

The Wardens are in their ring.

He has put them there himself, in the last four hours. It was not easy. They are slow, and old, and much given to a sort of grave, slow, wooden confusion. He has had to explain, through Pebble, in a long stream of small patient thoughts, exactly what he wanted. They are to stand along the pool's rim. They are to stand very still. They are not to move until he says. And when he does, they are to do what they have been waiting four hundred years to do, which is to keep a thorn out of the garden.

It says it understands, says Pebble. It says the thorn is a man.

Yes.

It says it has never met a man who was not a thorn.

That is not true. It met my father.

It says your father is a very small thorn, she reports, with great care, and it likes him anyway.

He almost laughs. He does not. He is looking at the gate Warden, vast and black at the head of the ring, with its granite shield on its arm and its amber lamp burning steady and quiet in the hollow of its face. It has not taken its eyes off the seam. It has been standing in the same place for six days without once shifting its weight.

It is the only one of us, he thinks, who is not afraid.

He reaches into his sleeve and takes out the Stone Skin talisman. It is the last of his father's. He unfolds it, and looks at it a moment, at the soft gray lines and the tiny, tired, perfect hand that drew them. Then he folds it again, and puts it away.

Not yet.

* * *

They come at the ninth hour.

He feels the seam before he sees it. It is a thin cold pressure at the back of his skull, like a finger laid on a bone, and then a long slow tremor in the moss, and then a faint sound: a high, thin, silvery whine, like a wire drawn through water. At the far end of the long avenue of herb beds, in the gray mist, a vertical line of green light flickers, and widens, and holds.

A man steps through it.

He is very tall. He wears black, from throat to heel, a long close-fitting robe with a high collar, and over the face a mask of pale bone, smooth and featureless, with two narrow slits for eyes. He moves without a sound. He does not look about him. He stands in the green light, perfectly still, with his hands folded, and lets the mist curl round his ankles, and waits.

A second follows. A third. A fourth.

They form a square. They are all alike, tall, black, masked, silent as stones. They stand with their backs to one another in the long gray rows, facing outward, like the four points of a compass, and for a long moment nothing at all happens.

Pool-stage, thinks Jian. Not Elder. But close.

They are, he knows, the men that Mei Ru did not name. The priests. The Wellmen. The Sect's inner guard, who are said to have drunk so deep of the old blood that they no longer cast shadows. He has watched them come through a seam, one by one, with a grave deliberate step, into a garden they have never seen, and not one of them has looked round.

They do not look, he thinks, because they have been told it is empty.

And last, in no hurry, through the green light, with a clay jar in one hand and a long thin package wrapped in black silk beneath his arm, comes Elder Mu.

* * *

He looks as he did in the quarry. That is the strangest thing. In the quarter-light of the garden he is simply a lean old man in a gray robe, with a stoop in his shoulders and ink on his cuff, and a face of such mild, such gentle, such scholarly sweetness that no one, seeing him in a library, would have looked twice. He stands at the mouth of the seam, with the mist about his knees, and looks up at the ceiling.

Then he lowers his eyes, and sees the boy.

"Ah," says Mu.

He does not hurry. He does not call his men. He comes down the long avenue between the beds, with the clay jar in his hand and the black package under his arm, as a man comes down a garden path on a summer afternoon. The four masked figures turn, in unison, and follow at a distance of ten paces. The Wardens do not move. The gate Warden's lamp burns very steady.

He stops, at last, at the foot of the terrace steps, thirty paces from the pool, and bows.

"Little boy," he says.

"Elder."

"You have kept the door open for me. I am touched." The soft voice is warm with real feeling. "I have been looking for it for sixty years, you know. I thought it would be a great deal harder to find."

"It was left," says Jian.

"I see that." The old man's eyes move over the Orchard, slowly, with a sort of tender hunger. They linger on the beds. They linger on the pool, and the pale broken plate on the terrace, and the great black Warden at the head of its ring. "It is very beautiful. I had not imagined. I thought a vault, a hall, a cold dark room full of bones. I did not think it would be a garden."

"No."

"A garden." Mu sighs. "How like him. How exactly like the old fox. He said once, in the Well, over a cup of wine, that the thing he was proudest of was a small round field, with a wall, where nothing was ever killed. I thought it was a joke." A small dry silence. "It seems that I was mistaken about a great many things."

He is stalling, thinks Jian. He is looking for the trap.

He does not move. He does not blink. He sits with his feet in the green water and the pale creature in his lap and the Veil, the last of it, drawn thin as a scrap of silk round the lump of fear in his chest.

"You have not asked," says Mu, pleasantly, "why I have come."

"For the door."

"For the door, yes. And for the pangolin, who I understand has recovered. I am glad. I was most uneasy about her." The mild eyes rest on Pebble. "And for you."

"For me?"

"I have not been able to forget you, little boy. It is a very rare thing. I have spent sixty years among clever men, and I have found that most of them are interesting for about a week. You have been interesting for two seasons." He smiles. "I should like to know what you are."

"I am a boy."

"No," says Mu, gently. "You are not. You are something that has been put into a boy. I felt it in the corpse." The smile does not change. "A bright cold shape, like a blade. It looked at me through the dead woman's eyes. It said I see you. And then it took my thread." He tilts his head. "It was the most remarkable sensation. I have been the Elder of the Well for forty years, and I have not been touched in thirty. I wept."

"I am sorry."

"Do not be. It was the best thing that has happened to me in a decade." The old man sets down the clay jar, with care, on the moss. "Which is why I am going to be so very sorry, in a moment, to kill you."

* * *

He does not signal. He does not need to. At some tiny unseen movement of the lean gray hand, the four masked figures begin to move.

They are very fast.

They come across the moss in a long low flicker, black and silent, with the pale masks gleaming, and Jian, who has been waiting six days for this, finds that he cannot think of a single plan. It is a strange thing. A great clear white stillness has come into his head, like snow in an empty room. He sits with his feet in the water and the pangolin in his arms and watches them come.

Now, he says.

He does not say it aloud. He says it to the moss, and the stone, and the old slow patience of the garden, with the whole of his small tired will. And the Wardens, eleven of them, in a ring round the pool, lift their heads.

It is not like a fight. It is like a landslide.

The first of the black men, a tall silent shape with a long curved blade in each hand, reaches the edge of the ring and does not stop. He goes through the gap between two of the smaller Wardens, light as a cat. He is three paces from Jian. The blades are lifted. And Limp, the lame one, the old gnarled thing with the dragging root, which has not once in six days moved a limb, simply puts out one long willow arm and closes it round his waist.

There is a sound like a branch breaking.

It is very quick. The man does not cry out. He hangs in the grip of the bark for a moment with his masked face turned down, as if looking in some mild surprise at the thing that has taken him. Then the arm closes, and the long robe goes limp, and Limp sets him down on the moss, quite gently, like a child laying a doll in a bed.

One, thinks Jian.

The second and third reach the great black Warden at the head of the ring. It does not move. It lifts its shield, a slab of gray granite as wide as a door. The two men strike it from opposite sides, with a clang like a bell, and rebound. They are Pool-stage. They have the speed, and the strength, and the cold exact skill of men who have killed for forty years. They hit the shield again. It does not give. It simply stands, as a mountain stands in a storm, and the amber lamp in the hollow of its head burns slow and steady, and from somewhere behind the stone, deep in the old hard heart, comes a long low hum.

It is a note he knows. It is the one he sang in the quarry, in the red dark, with his hand on the moss.

The Warden's fist comes down.

* * *

It is over in a minute.

He does not see all of it. He sees the second man crushed, with a short flat crunch, into the moss. He sees the third go over the pool's rim in a long arc, with a Warden's hand round his ankle, and vanish into the water without a sound. He sees the fourth, a lean, silent, graceful figure, slip through the line of the ring like a ghost, and run, in a long low zigzag, straight for the terrace.

He is going for the plate.

It is the wrong thing. It is the thing Jian has been afraid of for six days. A man who cannot get to the boy will go for the lock, and a man at the lock has the whole of the garden at his back. He lifts his hand. He opens his mouth to give the order.

And across the moss, quite calmly, with a clay jar in one hand and a black package under the other, Elder Mu says: "No."

The Wardens stop.

They stop all at once, as if a rope had been drawn through them. Their great slow limbs hang in mid-air. The little green lamps in their faces flicker, and gutter, and dim. And along the length of the black web of thread that runs from each of them down into the moss, a thin line of red light blooms, and begins to travel, upward, with a fine, dry, whispering sound, like fire in dry grass.

Overwrite.

Jian has read the word, and he has felt it, once, in a red garden, and he has not forgotten it. He reaches for the thread, with the third level's bright clarity, and he finds it. He finds it, and it is not the same. It is thicker. It is older. It has been laid down in the soil of the garden for a week, in tiny strands, in the roots of the beds, in the veins of the stone, and it does not come from a corpse. It comes from a man standing thirty paces away, with a gentle smile.

He did not take the Orchard, he thinks, in a long cold plunge. He seeded it.

"I am so sorry," says Mu. "I could not help myself. It is such a lovely trick. I have been laying it for a week, you know, at night, a thimble of blood in a thousand beds. I thought: if the boy has the hill, and the garden, and the beast, then I must have a hand inside the garden. It is only courteous." He lifts the jar. "I should so much prefer to do this the quiet way."

In the dim, the Wardens shudder.

* * *

He has three needles. He has a Stone Skin. He has a reserve of perhaps five units, and a bond with a very small tired creature that has lost two scales since the cellar, and a rib that has been broken twice and healed once. And he has, in the back of his mind, in the dark, a small flat white line that has been waiting for six days.

Separation: binding agent from host. Cost: scales.

He has never used it on a garden.

How much? he says.

Sixty-two.

He looks at the number for a long moment. He thinks of the half scroll, and a hundred thousand things the garden has not yet been asked. He thinks of his father on a stair, with a sword, and his mother on a terrace with a knife in each hand, and the three hundred and sixty-eight people on the moss behind him, drinking water from skins.

Everything has a cost, he thinks, and the words, for the first time, do not sound like a bill.

Yes.

* * *

It does not hurt, which is the worst of it.

The red threads go out of the Orchard in a single long bright sweep, like a held breath let go. He feels them leave. He feels them peel from the roots, from the stone, from the great slow hearts of the Wardens, a fine web of red light drawn up out of the earth and gathered into a single bright thread, thick as a rope, that runs from the garden to the lean gray man at its end. It is a very beautiful thing. It glitters.

Mu does not move. His face, for the first time, is quite blank.

"That," he says, "is not possible."

"It was a trap," says Jian.

"No. It is a thing that is not done." The mild voice has altered. There is something in it now, a thin hard edge like a fault in a mirror. "A garden is not a host. It has no blood. It cannot be separated. It is impossible."

"I know."

"Then how—"

"I do not know." And it is true. He is shaking all over. A great ringing sickness has come into his head, a high thin singing like a needle drawn along a plate, and the world at the edges of his vision has begun to go gray. "I only know that you put it there, and I took it out."

The rope of red goes taut. For a moment the two of them, the old man and the boy, hold the length of it between them. He sees Mu's hand tighten on the clay jar. He sees the lines come into the lean sweet face. He sees the long fine fingers of the left hand begin, slowly, to rise.

And behind the boy, in the green dark, eleven Wardens lift their heads.

The gate Warden is first. It does not walk; it goes, a black mountain in motion, up the terrace steps in three great strides. The fourth masked man has just reached the plate. He is kneeling, with a hand outstretched to the crack. The shield comes down on him from above like a closing door, and when it lifts, there is nothing on the black stone but a wide dark stain and a bone mask, cracked clean across.

Four, thinks Jian, in a long dull wonder. All four.

Mu has seen it too. His face does not change. But the rope of red light in his fist has begun to fray, and he is moving, slowly, backward, toward the one thing in the garden that is still his: the long gray line of the seam, hanging at the avenue's end.

He will run, thinks Jian. And he can. He is a Pool. He is faster than any of us.

He has one thing left. He has known it for six days. He has not wanted to use it, because it is the one thing in the garden that is not a trap but a gift, the thing that the Orchard was built round, and he does not know, even now, what it will cost.

He puts both palms on the rim of the reservoir.

The old wall is white stone, a hand's breadth thick, hollow in the heart with four centuries of seepage. Every thing has one, the stele said. The place where the thing is not. He pours into it the last of his reserve, a thin bright thread, and sings.

The pool's wall breaks along its whole eastern side.

It does not burst. It lets go. A long green wave rolls out over the moss, knee deep, pale, cold, thick with the Qi of four hundred years, and it runs down the avenue of beds in a single sheet, faster than a man can run. It strikes the old man's ankles. It strikes his knees. And Mu, who has drunk blood for sixty years and not once touched water that was alive, gives a thin sharp gasp and staggers, as a man staggers who has stepped from the dark into a blaze of light.

The blood-art in him recoils. Jian sees it. He sees the long red threads that cling to the old man's robes curl and blacken and run from the green like grease from a flame. For the space of one breath, one single breath, the Elder of the Well is slow.

That is enough, says Pebble, very small, from the rim of the pool.

* * *

Pebble.

Here.

Now.

She does not answer. She slides out of his lap and goes down the pool's rim in a quick low scuttle, small, bare, pale, like a leaf blown along a floor. She reaches the water's edge. She stops. She stands up on her hind legs, with her tiny hands lifted and her whole thin body bent like a bow, and sings.

It is the same note. It is a long high rising scale, and it does not stop. It goes on and on, and he feels her go with it, scale by scale, breath by breath, the whole of her small bright life poured out into a single sound.

The seam at the end of the avenue begins, slowly, to close.

Mu turns his head.

It is the first time he has looked away from the boy. He sees the thin green line begin to narrow, a hand's breadth, a finger, a thread. He sees the faint, clear, silver gleam of the tiny creature on the rim of the pool. He sees the Wardens, in their ring, moving at last, with the slow grave dignity of old stone, toward him.

He is thinking, Jian thinks, in the long white silence. He is thinking he can reach it.

He is right. He is very fast. He drops the jar. The long thin package falls from his arm, unnoticed, in the moss, and he flows, in a long gray blur, across thirty paces of garden. He reaches the avenue's end in the space of a breath, with one hand lifted and the other thrust out, to seize the closing light.

And the seam, which has been narrowing for a hundred heartbeats, a hand's breadth, a finger, a thread, stops.

It is not closed. It is held. A bright line, no wider than a hair, hangs in the air between the beds, with the cold wet breath of the hill coming out of it, and in it, at the level of the old man's heart, a small dark gap, perfectly clear.

He puts his hand through it.

Now, says Pebble.

And the seam shuts.

* * *

There is no sound.

It is not loud. It is only a small, clean, definite thing, a sort of click, like the closing of a box. There is a long, still, breathless pause. And then, from the avenue's end, a single thin cry, like the sound of a bird.

Jian does not look.

He cannot. He has fallen to his knees on the moss, with both hands pressed to his face, and the whole of his mind is a roaring white blank. The cold has gone out of his body. The ringing has stopped. Something small and bright and thin, that has been part of him for ten years, a quiet, still, silvery thing, like a veil of water laid over his thoughts, has parted, and torn, and gone.

The Veil, he thinks, from a long way off.

It was his. It was the one thing that was only his. He had learned it from his mother, in a snowbound night, with her cool hands on his, and it had been, in the whole of the cold dark world, the single place where he was not seen. And it is gone. He feels the lack of it as one feels the lack of a tooth, the raw bright hole of a thing taken out.

Pebble.

He gropes. His hand finds the moss, and the cold stones, and the pool's wet rim. It finds something small and still and very light. It is bare. It is shuddering. It has curled up so tight that it is a ball, with its tail over its nose.

Here, she says. It is almost nothing. It is a breath. Here. I am here.

He lifts her. He holds her against his chest, with his face in the bare place between her shoulders, and rocks. He does not know that he is weeping. Behind him, down the length of the avenue, the green light has gone out of the world, and a lean gray shape is lying on the moss, quite still, in two pieces, with one pale hand outflung on the black earth, palm up, as if asking for rain.

The gate Warden comes slowly down the steps.

It stops beside the boy. It lowers its great black head. In the hollow of its face the amber lamp has changed, as he watches, from a coal to a flame, and the flame is the color of new leaves. It does not speak. It lays one vast gentle hand upon his shoulder, and the whole of the garden, from the pool to the roof, begins very softly to hum.

Behind it, one by one, the others bow.
